  needed just to look at another branch. The first versions were fairly minimal:
  git worktree add created a new directory tied to a branch, and git worktree
  list showed what existed. Over the following releases the command gained more
  safeguards and conveniences. Git began refusing to check out the same branch
  in two worktrees unless forced, which prevented silent conflicts over a shared
  ref. Later versions added git worktree remove, git worktree prune for
  cleaning up entries whose directories had been deleted by hand, and git
  worktree lock for keeping a worktree on removable storage from being pruned.
  Support for per-worktree configuration arrived with extensions.worktreeConfig,
  which let settings differ between checkouts while still sharing the
  repository's common configuration. Tooling built on top of worktrees followed,
  including editor integrations and continuous integration scripts that spin up
  disposable checkouts for each job. Today the feature is a standard part of
  many workflows, especially for reviewing pull requests, running long builds in
  parallel with ongoing edits, and working on several releases at once without
  repeatedly rebuilding the same project from scratch.
